# The most profitable investment we can make

Colombia faces a crucial challenge: thousands of young people want access to higher education, but the conditions for doing so remain inadequate. The main barrier is not a lack of aspiration, but a lack of funding. In a context of stagnant enrollment and demographic change, expanding and diversifying access mechanisms is not only necessary: ​​it is, today, the most profitable investment we can make as a society.

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias)
- [Our Impact](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/nuestro-impacto)
- The Most Profitable Investment We Can Make

![Image: The most profitable investment we can make](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/360e0a63-7149-4123-964d-a3029687c3db/web/lainversionmasrentable.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=XJynwGAA)

**César Eduardo Tamayo Tobón,**

**Dean of the School of Finance, Economics and Government at EAFIT**

Colombia faces a troubling paradox today: thousands of young people want to study at a university, but as a society we are unable to offer them the conditions to do so. This is not simply a failure of the education system. Rather, it reflects a disconnect between our aspirations and the decisions we make regarding the funding of higher education.

The first symptom is stagnant coverage. After significant progress during the past decade, growth in access to higher education has slowed in recent years. Gross enrollment rose from 42% to 53% between 2012 and 2017, but only increased to around 57.5% in the following seven years, up to 2024. In fact, the absolute number of students has barely grown: undergraduate enrollment increased from around 2.2 million in 2017 to about 2.35 million in 2024.

This behavior is not due to decreased demand. Young people continue to value education and want access to it. According to the 2024 Education Opinion Survey by Empresarios por la Educación (Business Leaders for Education), 94% of young people consider education important, and 82% perceive it as useful for their lives. Their educational aspirations are broad and consistent. A significant proportion aspire to complete university studies, including postgraduate studies.

The problem, then, does not lie in the demand: the main barrier is funding. Sixty percent of young people cite a lack of resources as the primary reason why they cannot reach their desired level of education.

And indeed, the mechanisms for financing higher education, which have never been sufficient, have weakened even further in recent years. The combination that for years allowed for a systematic expansion of access—demand-side subsidies, student loans, and an increase in public offerings—now has less reach. Uncertainty surrounding student loans, the reduction of support programs, and the sluggishness of instruments such as scholarships have restricted the options available to young people.

The result is a system in which the burden of financing increasingly falls on families, many of whom are unable to afford it. This limits access and widens the gap between students from different income levels. In practice, the system ends up being more exclusionary than the aggregate coverage figures suggest.

In this context, the State cannot close the gap on its own. Colombia's current fiscal situation is critical, and any effort to strengthen public education will be insufficient to address the magnitude of the problem. Therefore, it is necessary to expand funding sources and diversify the available instruments.

Colombia lags significantly behind in philanthropy and impact investing for education funding. While in the United States philanthropic donations exceed 2% of gross domestic product (GDP), in Latin America this figure is several times lower, rarely reaching even 0.5%. In countries with a dynamic philanthropy market, a substantial portion of these resources goes to higher education. In the Anglo-Saxon system, for example, many universities finance between 20% and 40% of their budget through donations and returns from endowment funds. In Colombia, although some progress has been made, these mechanisms remain marginal.

A similar situation exists with impact investing, which in Colombia remains limited in scale. A recent measurement by Fedesarrollo (2025) finds that assets under management in this market range from US$1.2 billion to US$1.5 billion (between 0.3% and 0.4% of GDP), with only 55 active investors. Furthermore, it is a market concentrated among a few players, with a strong focus on sectors such as financial inclusion, energy, and agriculture, and in which education has a relatively marginal presence. All of this limits the development of instruments that could be particularly useful for expanding access to higher education, such as student loan programs or income-contingent loan models.

In practice, the country has few alternatives for financing the investment that could yield the highest returns. Recent studies on Colombia estimate that each additional year of higher education has a return of approximately 20%. Furthermore, greater investment in human capital increases productivity, facilitates social mobility, and strengthens innovation capacity. This is also a matter of growth and equity.

We must change our understanding of the problem. Funding for higher education cannot depend solely on the state or families. It must involve businesses, foundations, and investors, with mechanisms that allow resources to be channeled in a more stable and predictable way.

But this context is further complicated by a factor that changes the landscape of the problem: our accelerated demographic transition. Colombia is entering a stage where the young population will begin to decline significantly, closing a window of opportunity that the country has maintained for several decades. The figures are clear. Between 2025 and 2035, the population aged 17 to 21 will decrease by approximately 88,000 people. Between 2035 and 2045, the decline will be much greater, with nearly 500,000 fewer young people. At the same time, the proportion of dependents relative to the working-age population will increase.

This change has direct implications: each cohort of young people will be smaller. In this context, leaving a significant portion of them out of the system has a higher cost for the country. The loss of human capital becomes more difficult to compensate for. The problem is no longer just expanding coverage, but doing so within a shorter timeframe. The decisions made in this decade will define the country's capacity to adapt to these demographic changes and sustain its growth.

In short, the current situation combines stagnant coverage with weakening existing funding mechanisms, shallow philanthropy and low impact investment, and accelerated demographic change. We must address this with decisive action in support of higher education to prevent it from becoming a structural constraint on our ability to grow and prosper.

**20 would be the return of each additional year of schooling in higher education according to recent studies on Colombia.**

**The funding of higher education cannot depend solely on the State or families.**
